revealWordProblem.title: Apply: Wrapping the Time Capsule
revealWordProblem.text: A time capsule box is shaped like a rectangular prism that is 9 in long, 4 in wide, and 5 in tall. You unfold it into a net so you can see all six faces laid flat. How many square inches of wrapping paper are needed to cover the whole box? Explain your reasoning.
revealWordProblem.sampleAnswer: Unfolding the box into a net shows 3 pairs of faces. SA = 2(9×4) + 2(9×5) + 2(4×5) = 72 + 90 + 40 = 202. You need 202 in² of wrapping paper.

turnAndTalk.question: To find how much wrapping paper a time capsule box needs, why is unfolding it into a net more helpful than looking at the 3D box?
turnAndTalk.kernel: A net lays every face flat so you can see and measure all six faces.

stems.es: Una red ayuda porque muestra las ___ caras puestas ___.

turnAndTalk.question: For the box l = 8, w = 5, h = 3, you found three face pairs. How did you use the net to organize the faces into pairs, and which pair had the largest area?
turnAndTalk.kernel: Opposite faces match in size, so the six faces form three equal pairs.

stems.en: The faces come in ___ pairs because opposite faces are ___.

turnAndTalk.question: A gift box is 14 × 10 × 6 in and one sheet of paper covers 400 in². Talk through how to find how many sheets are needed to cover the whole box.
turnAndTalk.kernel: Find the surface area first, then divide by what one sheet covers and round up.

stems.en: The surface area is ___ in² because SA = 2(14×10) + 2(14×6) + 2(10×6).
stems.es: El área de superficie es ___ in² porque SA = 2(14×10) + 2(14×6) + 2(10×6).

turnAndTalk.listenFor: Students compute SA = 280 + 168 + 120 = 568 in², then 568 ÷ 400 = 1.42, and round up to 2 sheets to cover the whole box.
turnAndTalk.extend: Why must you round the number of sheets up instead of down, and what does the leftover paper represent?
extendStems: The leftover paper is about ___ in² because ___.

turnAndTalk.question: A classmate found the surface area of a box but only multiplied two of the three face pairs by 2. How would you explain why every pair must be doubled?
turnAndTalk.kernel: Each of the three face shapes appears twice on the box, so all three areas must be doubled.

stems.en: Every face pair must be multiplied by ___ because each shape appears ___ times.

stems.en: If you forget to double one pair, the surface area will be too ___.

turnAndTalk.listenFor: Students explain a prism has opposite congruent faces (three pairs), so SA = 2lw + 2lh + 2wh, and missing a '2' undercounts one whole face.
turnAndTalk.extend: How does looking at the net make it obvious that there should be six faces, not five? Generalize the rule.

conceptIntro.heading: Push further — How do we find the surface area of a box?
conceptIntro.intro: You already can do this. In this group we go deeper: trickier numbers, a second way to see it, and explaining why it works — not just getting the answer.
conceptIntro.keyIdea: A box has 3 pairs of matching faces, so add up all 6 faces to get the surface area. — and you can explain WHY, and predict when it gets tricky.

iDo.title: Watch me
lines: My box is 8 long, 5 wide, and 3 tall. I unfold it into a net and see 3 pairs of faces.
Top and bottom: each is 8 × 5 = 40, and there are 2 of them, so 2 × 40 = 80.
Front and back: each is 8 × 3 = 24, so 2 × 24 = 48.
Left and right: each is 5 × 3 = 15, so 2 × 15 = 30.
I add all the pairs: 80 + 48 + 30 = 158. The surface area is 158 in².

weDo.title: Generalize it
lines: Start from what you know: Now a smaller box: 4 long, 3 wide, 2 tall. How many pairs of faces does it have?
Now predict: what happens with much bigger numbers, or numbers that share no common factors? Make a prediction, then check it.

youDo.title: Take the challenge
lines: Work the challenge problems below. For each one, be ready to justify your answer to a skeptic.
If you finish early: find a second strategy, or a case where it would break.

explore.instructions: Go deeper: Identify each face of the rectangular time capsule box (l = 8 in, w = 5 in, h = 3 in). Find the area of each face pair, then calculate the total surface area. As you work, ask yourself WHY it works.

discourse.prompt: The total surface area is 158 in². Which face pair contributes the most area? Why does that make sense when you look at the dimensions?
discourse.sentenceFrame: The ___ faces contribute the most area (___ in²) because their dimensions ___ × ___ = ___ are the largest. The total SA is ___ + ___ + ___ = ___ in².

onLevel.stem: A cube has edges of 5 cm. What is its surface area?
onLevel.explanation: A cube has 6 identical faces. Each face: 5 × 5 = 25 cm². Total SA = 6 × 25 = 150 cm².
choiceFeedback: That's the volume calculation (edge cubed) — surface area needs six face areas added together.
Check the units — a flat surface is measured in square units, not cubic.
Square the edge length for one face's area first, then multiply by the number of faces.
hints: A cube's 6 faces are identical squares, each one 5 cm by 5 cm.
Find the area of one square face, then multiply by 6 — and keep square units (cm²).
One face is 5 × 5 = 25 cm². Now multiply that area by the number of faces, 6.

onLevel.title: Spot the Mistake — One Pair Was Not Doubled

workedExample.label: Read
workedExample.work: A time capsule box from the net is l = 7 in, w = 5 in, h = 4 in. Find the surface area.

onLevel.correctWork: The student doubled the first two pairs but forgot to double the left/right pair. There are two 20 in² faces, so it should be 2(20) = 40, not 20. Correct: SA = 70 + 56 + 40 = 166 in².
hints: Every face pair has 2 matching faces — check that each area is multiplied by 2.
The left and right faces are both 5×4 = 20, so add 40 in², not 20 in².

extending.title: Find the Surface Area Error

workedExample.label: Dimensions
workedExample.work: l = 10 in, w = 4 in, h = 3 in

extending.correctWork: The student forgot to multiply the last face pair by 2. It should be 2(4×3) = 24, not 12. Correct: SA = 80 + 60 + 24 = 164 in².
hints: Check Step 3: how many times does each face pair appear?
Each face pair has 2 matching faces. The student only counted one left/right face.

extending.prompt: Two boxes have the same volume of 60 in³. Box A is 5 × 4 × 3. Box B is 10 × 6 × 1. Which box uses less wrapping paper (has less surface area)? Show your calculations and explain why a more cube-like shape might use less material.
extending.sentenceFrame: Box A: SA = 2(___) + 2(___) + 2(___) = ___ in². Box B: SA = 2(___) + 2(___) + 2(___) = ___ in². Box ___ uses less wrapping paper because ___.
extending.hint: Find three different factor combinations of the target volume.
hints: Both boxes hold 60 in³, but wrapping paper depends on SURFACE AREA — the outside covering, not the inside space.
Compute SA = 2lw + 2lh + 2wh for each box, then compare the two totals before you explain.
Box A first: faces are 5×4 = 20, 5×3 = 15, and 4×3 = 12. Double each and add, then repeat for Box B's faces.

extending.instructions: Compare volume and surface area. Which measurement is bigger for each prism?
extending.hint: Use the formula V = length × width × height for each row.
hints: Each row is a cube. Volume is edge × edge × edge; surface area is 6 × (edge × edge). Compare the two numbers.
Fill both columns for each cube, then write which NUMBER is larger. Watch what happens as the cubes get bigger.
For the 2 × 2 × 2 cube: volume is 2 × 2 × 2, and SA is 6 × (2 × 2). Compute both and compare them.

optional.stem: You unfold a time capsule that is a cube. Its net shows 6 equal squares, and each square has an area of 4 cm². What is the cube's total surface area?
optional.explanation: A cube net has 6 equal square faces. With each face 4 cm², the surface area is 6 × 4 = 24 cm².
choiceFeedback: Multiply the face area by all six faces — don't just add the face count to the area.
A cube net has six faces, not four — multiply the face area by six.
Some faces are easy to forget in a net — make sure you count and include all six squares.

optional.stem: Your team unfolds a rectangular time capsule box into a flat net. How many faces (flat sides) will the net show in all?
optional.explanation: A rectangular prism has 6 faces — top, bottom, front, back, left, and right — so its net shows 6 faces.
choiceFeedback: Don't forget the top and bottom faces — a box has faces all the way around.
Check again — did you count the face directly opposite the one you started with?
That's close to the number of corners (vertices), not the number of flat faces.

optional.stem: A time capsule box measures 2 in × 3 in × 4 in. Using its net, you add up all six faces. What is the total surface area?
choiceFeedback: That's the volume calculation — surface area needs the sum of all six face areas instead.
Make sure every face pair is doubled — a box has two of each of the three face shapes.
Doubling the volume isn't the same as adding up the six face areas — calculate each face separately.

practice.commonMistake: A common mistake in Surface Area Using Nets is finding the area of only one face from each of the 3 matching pairs and forgetting to double it, instead of counting all 6 faces. For a box that is 9 in × 4 in × 5 in, a student might add just one face from each pair: (9×4) + (9×5) + (4×5) = 36 + 45 + 20 = 101 in², but the net actually has two of each face, so the correct total is 2(36) + 2(45) + 2(20) = 72 + 90 + 40 = 202 in² — exactly double. Before you submit, ask: 'Did I count both matching faces in each pair, or only one from each pair?'

smallGroup.label: Challenge
smallGroup.who: Pull students who showed mastery on the formative check and are ready to extend.
moves: Launch the challenge fast — skip the re-teach, they don't need it.
Step back. Let them wrestle; protect the productive struggle.
Ask "How do you know?" and "Can you show it a second way?" more than you explain.
Push for a generalization: when does this hold, and when would it break?
Close by having one student justify a claim to the group.
